Series::ldexp¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::ldexp(const Series& other) const
Series Series::ldexp(double other) const
Series& Series::ldexp_(const Series& other)
Series& Series::ldexp_(const Series& rhs) const

What It Does¶

Scales each element by a power of two:

ldexp(x, e) = x * 2^e

x is the receiver; the argument supplies the exponent e. When e is an integer this is an exact binary shift of the exponent field — no rounding of the significand — which is why ldexp is the exact inverse of frexp(): mantissa.ldexp(exponent) rebuilds the original value. A non-integer e is allowed and gives the continuous x * 2^e.

The result is floating-point: an integer input is promoted (Float64 for integral or Float64 input, Float32 for Float32).

Parameters¶

other (const Series& or double): the exponent e. A Series broadcasts against the receiver; a double applies the same exponent everywhere.

Returns¶

Series or Series& x * 2^e, floating-point. ldexp_() writes the result back into the receiver.

Gradient¶

ldexp() is differentiable with respect to x:

d/dx ldexp(x, e) = 2^e

For a Series exponent, both operands are differentiable:

d/dx ldexp(x, e) = 2^e
d/de ldexp(x, e) = x * 2^e * ln(2)

The scalar overload has no Series exponent to receive sensitivity.

In-Place Form¶

ldexp_() is the in-place sibling of ldexp(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — ldexp_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.0}, {2});
auto y = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0}, {2});

x.ldexp_(y);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 8]

Examples¶

Example 1. Positive, zero, and negative exponents.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.5, 3.0}).ldexp(pluss::make_series({3, 0, -1})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[8.0000, 1.5000, 1.5000]

1 * 2^3 = 8, 1.5 * 2^0 = 1.5, 3 * 2^-1 = 1.5.

Example 2. A scalar exponent applies to every element.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).ldexp(2.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4.0000, 8.0000, 12.0000]

Example 3. The backward scales the sensitivity by 2^e.

auto x = pluss::make_series({3.0, 5.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.ldexp(pluss::make_series({1, 2})).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 4]

d/dx (x * 2^1) = 2 and d/dx (x * 2^2) = 4.

Example 4. A fractional Series exponent is continuous and receives sensitivity.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
auto e = pluss::make_series({0.5, -1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
e.tracks_slope_(true);
x.ldexp(e).sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity()) << '\n';
pluss::series::print(std::cout, e.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.4142, 0.5000]
Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.9605, 1.0397]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The result is always floating-point; an integer x is promoted.

  • A floating Series exponent carries gradient; an integer exponent cannot track slope.

  • ldexp_() accepts a Series exponent, requires a floating receiver, and preserves the receiver’s existing storage and shape.

  • A very large e overflows to +/-inf and a very small one underflows to 0, the same as any float multiply.

  • ldexp is the inverse of frexp(); round-tripping is exact for integer exponents.

Summary¶

ldexp(x, e) is x * 2^e:

  • exponent may be a Series or a scalar; integer exponents are exact shifts

  • result is floating-point

  • differentiable in x and a floating Series exponent

  • the inverse of frexp(); ldexp_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::frexp: the inverse — split x into (mantissa, exponent).

  • Series::exp2: 2^x, the continuous power-of-two.

  • Series::mul: the underlying scale.
